title: Reading Kulli material culture without inventing a kingdom
summary: Kulli describes a recognisable archaeological complex, not a kingdom whose borders and rulers are known. Settlement surveys reveal both shared forms and significant local differences.

body.text: Kulli is a useful archaeological term, but it can become misleading when treated as the name of a known kingdom. Recognisable objects and settlement patterns do not automatically supply a ruler, a capital or a political boundary. The term allows researchers to discuss relationships within material culture while leaving those larger social questions open.

Ute Franke-Vogt’s account of fieldwork in southeastern Balochistan explains that the complex takes its name from the site of Kulli in Kolwa, investigated by Aurel Stein. Her team’s surveys found a substantial range of settlements associated with this material. Some occupied elevated positions; others formed compact groups on open ground.
Shared forms, different settlements

The survey describes arrangements of houses, lanes and terraces, with stone used in substantial construction. It also records dams associated with many settlements. This evidence widens the discussion beyond painted pots and animal imagery. Kulli-related communities were making places as well as objects.

Variation within those places is important. A hilltop settlement and an open hamlet may participate in related practices without serving identical functions. Size, setting and internal arrangement should be considered before drawing conclusions about their relationship. A shared ceramic label is not a complete settlement hierarchy.

Nindowari provides one substantial archaeological point of reference. The official catalogue records excavation under Jean-Marie Casal. Its place in a researched landscape should not, however, turn it automatically into the capital of an imagined Kulli state. That would require a different kind of argument.
Where categories overlap

Franke-Vogt’s discussion of Bakkar Buthi is particularly instructive. The site’s assemblage is predominantly Harappan in character but also includes Kulli elements. Excavated building phases and pottery-production waste add further context. The combination does not fit a simple map divided into mutually exclusive cultural territories.

An assemblage can contain objects made through different traditions. Those objects might reflect exchange, local production, learning or several processes together. Choosing between these explanations requires attention to manufacture and context rather than treating the presence of a motif as a passport stamp.
What would demonstrate political organisation?

Questions about power remain legitimate. Differences in settlement scale, access to resources and investment in buildings may contribute to an interpretation. But each observation needs to be related to the others, and alternative explanations should be considered. Architectural prominence alone does not reveal a king’s name or the extent of his authority.

The same restraint should shape visual presentation. A map can show known sites and the distribution of material without drawing a hard border around a hypothetical kingdom. A caption can identify a Kulli-associated vessel without assigning its maker a language that has not been established.

Kulli’s importance does not depend on becoming a smaller version of a better-known civilisation. Its settlements and objects reveal a varied regional world with connections beyond it. Keeping the category flexible enough to accommodate that evidence makes the history more substantial, not less impressive.

title: Togau pottery and the challenge of dating regional change
summary: Togau pottery is recognised through a history of classification and comparison. Its decorative groups are useful research tools, but uncertain contexts prevent them from functioning as a simple universal clock.

body.text: Togau pottery is often introduced through recognisable painted designs, but its real archaeological interest lies in how those designs have been classified and dated. A sequence of motifs can look like a ready-made clock. It only becomes a reliable chronological tool, however, when the material has been connected to secure archaeological contexts.

The official catalogue identifies Togau as a site in the Kalat region, named after a nearby hamlet. The relationship between a type-site and the pottery category named after it should be kept clear. The category can occur at many places; it is not confined to the settlement whose name it carries.
How the categories were built

Zahir Hussain and Kiran Shahid Siddiqui’s analytical study explains the importance of Beatrice de Cardi’s work at Anjira and Siah Damb in defining Togau groups. Decorative differences were used to distinguish stages conventionally labelled A, B, C and D. The authors also note difficulties caused by erosion and the need to combine evidence from different excavations.

Their own survey observations in Panjgur found an uneven distribution of these types: some were prominent, others scarce or not clearly identified. Such variation matters. A group missing from a surface collection does not necessarily prove that the corresponding period was absent from the settlement.

Surface visibility, sample size and the locations examined can all shape what enters a collection. A classification is strongest when its limits are stated alongside its diagnostic features. Otherwise, a useful comparison can harden into an assumption that every region followed the same sequence at the same pace.
Context is part of the object

The study also discusses Togau-type vessels in a private collection and acknowledges their likely illicit excavation. Attractive, relatively complete vessels may preserve decoration while losing the information needed to date their deposition. Recovering an object from the market cannot recover the layer from which it was removed.

A contrasting example of documentation appears in Cambridge’s Museum of Archaeology and Anthropology. Its record for worked stone from Siah Damb includes an accession number, excavation information and a period attribution linked to de Cardi’s work. The object is not pottery, but the record shows how different kinds of finds can remain connected to an investigated sequence.
A chronology open to testing

For Togau, the productive question is therefore not which motif looks oldest in isolation. It is how decorative groups relate to manufacturing methods, associated finds and independently dated deposits. New evidence may confirm parts of an established sequence while requiring other parts to be revised.

This makes the pottery more than a set of pleasing designs. It becomes evidence for how researchers construct regional histories from incomplete material. A careful public account should show the beauty of the vessels while making clear that their chronological value depends on relationships that an unprovenanced object, however impressive, cannot supply on its own.

title: Why an unexcavated mound is still evidence
summary: A mound can preserve valuable evidence before excavation. Surface survey and geophysics ask different questions, and their results should guide careful research rather than turn an archaeological place into a treasure target.

body.text: An unexcavated mound is not an empty page. Its shape, surface material and relationship to the surrounding landscape can already provide evidence. What it does not provide is unrestricted permission to imagine the buildings, people or events beneath it. The challenge is to ask questions that the available methods can answer without pretending that investigation has already revealed everything.

Surface survey offers one starting point. Sidra Gulzar’s study of Ganweriwala explains how systematic examination of a site can record landscape, settlement form and the distribution of material. Such work can help researchers plan later investigation. Ganweriwala has now been excavated; its earlier survey remains a useful example of knowledge produced before trenches were opened.
Seeing a pattern without removing a layer

A concentration of pottery or building material can identify an area worth closer study. It does not automatically mark the precise boundary of an ancient house or workshop. Material may have moved through erosion, cultivation or later activity, and different parts of a surface may be unequally visible.

Recording those conditions is therefore part of the evidence. A map of finds without information about how the survey was conducted can suggest a precision it does not possess. Repeated observations and a documented collection strategy make comparison more meaningful.
What geophysics measures

Historic England explains that the choice of geophysical technique depends on the expected target, its depth, the area to be covered and local conditions such as soils, geology and vegetation. There is no single instrument that reveals every kind of archaeological feature equally well.

Oxford’s introduction makes another essential point: geophysical plots represent measured physical properties, such as electrical resistance or magnetism. They are not direct photographs of the past. A striking pattern may suggest a wall, ditch or other feature, but interpretation has to consider alternative explanations and the limits of the survey.

An apparently blank result is equally easy to overread. Failure to detect a feature with one method does not establish that no archaeology exists. The question is whether the chosen technique and conditions were suitable for the kinds of remains being sought.
Preservation is an active decision

Leaving deposits in place can preserve relationships that future research may examine with better methods or different questions. Excavation is not the only meaningful sign that a site matters. Documentation, monitoring and protection from disturbance can be substantial forms of archaeological work.

For a heritage atlas, the term unexcavated should therefore describe a dated research status, not a promise of hidden treasure. It should never encourage casual digging or collecting. Related sites may illustrate different stages of investigation rather than all sharing the same status.

A mound’s value lies in the information it contains and the questions it can help answer. Recognising that value before excavation is one of the clearest ways to move from curiosity about ancient objects toward care for archaeological evidence.

title: Layers, cuts and fills: a first guide to stratigraphy
summary: Stratigraphy reconstructs the order of archaeological events, including material added and ground removed. A simple hypothetical pit shows why depth alone cannot date a find.

body.text: Imagine a courtyard floor, a pit dug through it and soil later placed inside the pit. The floor came first, the digging happened next and the filling followed. All three belong to the archaeological sequence, but only two involve material added to the ground. The pit cut records removal. This simple example explains why stratigraphy is more than a stack of coloured layers.

Archaeologists study the relationships between deposits, structures and cuts to reconstruct an order of events. A context is an individually recorded unit within that work. The terminology may sound technical, but its purpose is practical: to preserve observations clearly enough that another researcher can examine the argument.
A cut and its fill are not the same event

Historic England’s recording manual distinguishes a cut from the deposits that fill it. The shape of a pit belongs to the event that created the hollow; material inside may have accumulated through one or several later episodes. Treating both as a single undifferentiated feature would conceal that sequence.

Return to the hypothetical courtyard. An old pottery fragment could be included in the soil used to fill the later pit. Its age would not make the pit older than the floor it cuts. The object’s manufacture and its final deposition are different moments.

This is why depth alone is unreliable. The bottom of a later pit can lie below an earlier floor. Without recording the cut, a deep find may appear older simply because it lies lower. The physical relationship corrects that misleading impression.
Turning observations into an ordered argument

A Harris matrix represents earlier and later relationships in a diagram. Historic England’s guidance emphasises direct stratigraphic relationships and warns against adding connections that the evidence does not establish. The diagram is not a picture of the trench; it is an account of sequence.

Two deposits at similar heights need not be contemporary. Conversely, parts of one deposit may be exposed in separate areas. Connecting them requires evidence and a stated basis, not just a convenient line on a chart. Where a relationship cannot be established, leaving the question open is more accurate than forcing an uninterrupted sequence.
Why the paperwork matters

The Museum of London’s field manual explains that excavation removes the contexts being investigated. Written descriptions, drawings, photographs and records of finds and samples therefore become essential evidence after the deposits are gone. Recording is not an administrative task added after discovery; it is part of the research itself.

The hypothetical courtyard could support several later questions about rebuilding, use or abandonment. Those questions would be impossible to revisit if the pit and floor had simply been cleared without recording their relationship.

Stratigraphy gives archaeological stories their sequence. It does not supply every date or explain every motive, but it establishes constraints that interpretations must respect. Learning to distinguish a layer, a cut and a fill is a first step toward understanding why careful excavation produces knowledge rather than merely exposing old things.

title: Radiocarbon dates are ranges, not birthdays
summary: Radiocarbon dating estimates the age of a sampled organism, not automatically the founding year of a settlement. Calibration, context and reported uncertainty are essential parts of the result.

body.text: A radiocarbon result is sometimes turned into a headline announcing the exact age of a building or civilisation. That shortcut loses two essential distinctions. The laboratory measures a sample, and the result has uncertainty. Connecting it to a historical event requires an archaeological argument as well as a measurement.

Oxford’s radiocarbon guidance explains that the method concerns carbon incorporated while an organism was alive. After death, radioactive decay changes the amount remaining. The resulting measurement is conventionally expressed in radiocarbon years before 1950, with an uncertainty. In this terminology, present does not move forward with the date on today’s calendar.
Why calibration is necessary

The amount of radiocarbon in the atmosphere has not remained constant. A radiocarbon age is therefore not simply a calendar year waiting to be subtracted from 1950. Calibration compares the result with material of known age to estimate possible calendar dates.

Oxford’s explanation shows why this can produce more than one likely calendar interval. The shape of the calibration curve matters, as does measurement uncertainty. Reporting only a midpoint can hide the actual distribution and create an impression of precision that the analysis does not support.

Historic England’s guidance recommends stating the calibration method and curve, together with the probability associated with the reported range. A range without its probability is incomplete information. The uncertainty is not an embarrassing weakness to remove; it is part of what the result means.
Which event has been dated?

Consider a hypothetical timber reused in a later structure. Dating its carbon would not automatically date the rebuilding. The relationship between the tree’s growth, the cutting of the timber and its eventual deposition would have to be considered. The same general question applies whenever sampled material may be older than the context in which it was found.

A short-lived sample securely associated with an event can answer a different question from unidentified charcoal in mixed soil. Neither should be described simply as the date of the site. Sample identification and context belong beside the number in any serious interpretation.
Results that can be checked again

Historic England also stresses retaining the laboratory identifier, the uncalibrated result and its uncertainty. Calibration curves are refined over time, so a future researcher may need to revisit the calculation. A polished timeline that preserves only a rounded calendar year makes that work harder.

For readers encountering early settlements such as Mehrgarh, the practical lesson is to ask what was sampled, where it came from and how the published date is expressed. A revised estimate need not mean that the site’s importance has disappeared; it may mean that the evidence has become better understood.

Radiocarbon dating is powerful precisely because its assumptions and uncertainties can be examined. Treating dates as supported ranges rather than birthdays allows scientific evidence to strengthen history without pretending that it offers a certainty beyond its reach.

title: Seeds from a trench: what archaeobotany asks
summary: Plant remains can reveal crop processing, fuel use and labour as well as food. Research at Harappa shows why seeds in a deposit should not be read as a straightforward ancient menu.

body.text: A charred seed from an excavation can seem like a direct message from an ancient meal. It may be evidence of food, but its route into the deposit needs investigation. A seed could arrive with processing waste, spilled grain, stored material or fuel. Archaeobotany asks how plants were used and how their remains survived, not merely which familiar foods can be named.

A recent study of Harappa makes that distinction especially clear. The researchers examined relationships between grain and weed seeds in the assemblage. Their analysis suggests that crops often reached the city in an already well-processed condition, while burning animal dung introduced many small weed seeds into archaeological deposits.
The route from field to sample

That interpretation changes what a collection of seeds can mean. Small weeds need not represent plants deliberately gathered for human consumption. They may have passed through animals and entered a fire as part of fuel. The material still reveals human activity, but the activity is different from the one suggested by a simple food list.

The Harappa study also records analytical limitations, including the difficulty of distinguishing some modern and ancient seeds without breaking them. Such decisions affect which material enters the final analysis. A published result is therefore inseparable from the procedures used to select and identify the evidence.

This makes the sample record important. Where was the material found? How much sediment was examined? What was preserved and what was excluded? These questions help prevent a very small or unusual group of remains from being treated as representative of an entire city.
Looking beyond visible seeds

Kashyap and Weber’s pilot study at Farmana in Haryana explored a complementary form of evidence: microscopic starch grains. They examined surfaces including pottery, stone tools and dental calculus. Their report argues that reliance on larger charred remains alone can overlook plants whose useful parts do not readily survive that process.

The Farmana work identified starches associated with several plant groups and linked observations to particular sampled surfaces. Those findings belong to Farmana; they should not be moved into Harappa’s record merely because both sites are associated with the Indus civilisation. The methodological comparison is valuable without inventing an identical diet.
From ingredients to work

Plant remains can also raise questions about where labour took place. If crops arrived at a settlement after substantial processing, some work may have occurred elsewhere. Establishing that possibility does not identify every worker or the terms of their labour, but it gives the investigation a more social dimension than a list of crops alone.

The strongest public account therefore follows evidence through a chain of reasoning. Identification comes first, then consideration of preservation and deposition, and only then an interpretation of practice. Seeds can reveal a great deal, but they do not speak in complete recipes. Their value lies in the careful questions that make ordinary fragments informative about ancient lives.

title: Animal bones and the limits of ancient menus
summary: Animal bones record more than meals. Species, skeletal parts, modification and deposition must be considered together before reconstructing husbandry, hunting or food consumption.

body.text: A pile of animal bones is not an ancient menu preserved in shorthand. Some remains may come from food preparation, but others can reflect craftwork, natural death, deliberate burial or later disturbance. Zooarchaeology begins by identifying the material and its context before deciding which human activities it represents.

Historic England’s animal-bone handbook sets out the importance of recording species, skeletal parts, age indicators and modifications. Cut marks can contribute evidence for carcass processing, while weathering and scavenger damage help reconstruct what happened before burial. These observations need to be considered together rather than allowing one dramatic mark to determine the whole interpretation.
What is being counted?

Fragment numbers are affected by breakage. One bone can produce many pieces, and different parts of a skeleton preserve differently. A count of fragments therefore cannot be converted directly into the number of animals eaten, still less into portions served to a population.

The handbook also emphasises that some processing activities leave more visible traces than others. An absence of cut marks is not automatically evidence that a carcass was untouched. Recording methods, preservation and the parts recovered all influence the result.

This is one reason that recovery procedures matter. If small bones are missed, the apparent balance between large animals and smaller species can change. The assemblage is not simply what once existed; it is what survived, was recovered and could be identified.
Availability is not the same as use

Richard Meadow’s discussion of regional subsistence offers a useful comparison from Balakot. He notes that fish bones and mollusc shells were uncommon in earlier levels but much more abundant in the later Harappan phase. Proximity to coastal resources did not produce an identical pattern of exploitation throughout the site’s history.

Meadow also stresses variation between settlements and phases, even where a broad agricultural foundation appears similar. Landscape creates possibilities and constraints, but people’s knowledge and decisions shape how those resources are used. An environmental map cannot by itself reconstruct a community’s diet.
Animals had lives before they became remains

Food is only one dimension of human-animal relationships. A study may also ask about management, movement, working lives or the use of non-food products. Those questions require evidence appropriate to them. Naming cattle in an assemblage does not, on its own, establish a particular dairy system or method of traction.

For early farming places such as Mehrgarh, this distinction helps keep the discussion grounded. The aim is not to project modern menus or identities backward, but to understand the relationships supported by the material.

An accessible archive article can explain the difference between identification and interpretation through a few well-recorded examples. The bones become more informative when their limitations are visible. Rather than offering a supposedly complete dinner table, they can reveal changing practices, selective survival and the work required to turn fragments into a history of human and animal lives.

title: What changing brick sizes can and cannot prove
summary: Indus brick proportions reveal shared building practices, but they do not by themselves prove a central building authority. Dimensions, reuse and construction context all affect the interpretation.

body.text: A brick is an unusually modest object on which to build a large historical claim. Yet the proportions of Indus bricks are frequently used to discuss standardisation, urban organisation and political authority. The evidence is important, but the steps between a measured object and a model of government need to remain visible.

The CSMVS museum’s record for a fired-clay brick from Moenjodaro introduces the familiar relationship of four to two to one in length, width and thickness. It also distinguishes examples of different absolute sizes. This is the first essential point: a ratio can remain similar while the dimensions change.
Proportion is not a single size

A small and a large rectangle can share the same proportions without being interchangeable building units. Recording only a ratio therefore loses information. Measurements, material, condition and architectural context should be retained so that comparisons can be checked.

J. Mark Kenoyer’s study of Harappan measurement discusses variation in brick sizes and the difficulties created by reuse. Fired bricks could be incorporated into later structures, separating their manufacture from the date of the wall in which they were found. A wall containing old bricks is not necessarily an old wall.

Kenoyer also cautions against treating uniform proportions as straightforward proof of a powerful central government enforcing building codes. Shared technical practices can spread through mechanisms other than a single administrative command. The existence of a pattern and the explanation for that pattern are separate propositions.
What a change might mean

A change in dimensions could relate to production, building requirements, repair or the reuse of available material. It might also form part of a broader social change. The point is not that political interpretation is impossible, but that a measurement alone cannot choose among all these explanations.

The strongest argument would examine a securely dated sequence of structures and compare evidence from more than one area. If measurements are taken from loose rubble or mixed deposits, the uncertainty should be stated. A graph can look precise while combining bricks that never belonged to the same building episode.
Looking at the work of building

The museum record draws attention to the interlocking arrangement of bricks in walls. This reminds us that a unit was designed to work with others. Proportion has practical consequences for joining courses and negotiating corners; it is not only an abstract symbol of order.

Specialised shapes raise further questions about particular construction tasks. Rather than forcing every brick into one ideal standard, a useful study asks what a builder needed the unit to do. Material choices and placement can be as informative as dimensions.

Indus brickwork remains impressive when these qualifications are retained. Its value is not weakened by abandoning an automatic equation between standardisation and central power. Careful measurement can reveal shared knowledge, variation and repeated rebuilding, allowing a commonplace object to illuminate urban life without making it carry more historical certainty than it can support.

title: Indus exchange without a modern trade map
summary: Evidence for Indus exchange can connect materials to sources without revealing the exact route or terms of a transaction. Geological and isotope studies help distinguish different kinds of movement.

body.text: A map of ancient exchange often uses arrows that resemble modern shipping routes. The arrows are easy to understand, but they can imply more than the evidence establishes. An object may connect a settlement with a raw-material source without telling us which path it followed, how many hands it passed through or what was exchanged for it.

Randall Law’s study of Harappa’s rock and mineral assemblage provides a useful alternative. It compares archaeological material with samples from potential geological sources. The resulting connections are not all presented with the same confidence. His summary distinguishes firm analytical assignments from reasonable but less directly tested inferences.
A line is an argument

Law explicitly explains that the pathways drawn on his maps are conjectural. A solid line can indicate strong evidence for a material-source relationship without documenting the exact road, river journey or coastal passage. This is a small cartographic distinction with large consequences for interpretation.

The study of steatite illustrates why source research is necessary. Potential deposits occur in several regions, and appearance alone cannot securely choose among them. Comparing the archaeological objects with geological samples supplies a more disciplined basis for an acquisition argument.

Even a strong match does not reveal the complete transaction. Material might move directly, through intermediaries or after being partly worked. Those possibilities require other evidence. A map should not silently turn a source attribution into proof that a named city controlled a distant quarry.
Objects and people leave different traces

A 2013 study by Kenoyer, Price and Burton explored another approach: isotope analysis of tooth enamel from individuals buried at Harappa and Ur. Its published abstract presents the work as a preliminary investigation of whether non-local people and movement could be identified more directly.

That is a different question from the geological origin of a bead. The movement of an object does not require its maker to travel with it, and the movement of a person does not identify their occupation. An isotope result should not be converted into a biography of a merchant without further support.
What exchange evidence can make visible

Taken together, these approaches widen the history beyond a list of exotic goods. They can illuminate changing access to materials, connections between regions and the mobility of people. They also reveal how much remains unknown about the institutions and everyday arrangements through which those connections operated.

For an atlas reader, a useful exchange map would identify the kind of evidence behind each connection and the period to which it belongs. It would separate a confirmed material source from a suggested route and avoid combining many centuries into one supposedly simultaneous network.

The Indus world does not need a modern-looking trade diagram to appear connected. Its relationships become more compelling when the evidence is allowed to retain different levels of certainty. A carefully explained line can then open a question about movement instead of closing it with an invented itinerary.

title: Meluhha: reading a name across different kinds of evidence
summary: Meluhha connects Mesopotamian texts with arguments about the Indus world. The name, a translator’s seal and traded objects are complementary evidence, not a decipherment of the Indus script.

body.text: Meluhha is a name encountered in Mesopotamian written evidence, not a word securely read from an Indus inscription. That distinction is essential. The name is widely associated with the Indus region in discussions of third-millennium BCE connections, but the association rests on an argument combining texts, geography and material evidence.

Gregory Possehl’s discussion of the Middle Asian interaction sphere places Meluhha alongside Dilmun and Magan in cuneiform accounts of maritime connections. He notes Sargon’s claim that ships from these places reached Akkad. Such references establish that Mesopotamian writers imagined and described a wider world, but they do not provide a modern map with surveyed boundaries.
The translator and the seal

One particularly evocative object is the cylinder seal of Shu-ilishu, identified in its inscription as an interpreter associated with Meluhha. Possehl’s separate account explains how the reading was checked again with a fresh impression. The episode makes scholarly verification visible: even a familiar object can benefit from returning to the original evidence.

The same account retains an important limitation. The seal came through a nineteenth-century collection with little archaeological findspot information. Its inscription is meaningful, but the missing excavation context restricts what can be said about precisely where it was used or deposited.

An interpreter’s existence suggests communication across a linguistic difference. It does not tell us everything about the language involved, the interpreter’s origins or the range of situations in which he worked. Those are tempting biographical questions, but the object does not answer them all.
Reading different evidence together

Objects found beyond the Indus region strengthen the broader discussion of contact. Possehl also describes how early classifications of seals required revision as archaeology in the Persian Gulf became better understood. Some pieces once grouped together because they looked Indian belonged to more complicated regional traditions.

This is why a resemblance and a written place-name should not simply be added together as if they were identical kinds of proof. An inscription can name a place; an object can preserve materials, techniques and imagery. Their relationship has to be demonstrated, with attention to date and archaeological context.

The electronic Sumerian dictionary’s entry for Meluhha provides a further reminder that the name belongs to a textual corpus. Its written occurrences can be studied without assuming that every use across all periods carried exactly the same geographical meaning.
Not a shortcut to decipherment

Possehl’s seal study explicitly distinguishes the readable cuneiform inscription from the undeciphered Indus writing system. The possibility that future bilingual evidence might help is not the same as possessing such a text. A translator mentioned in one script does not supply translations for signs in another.

Meluhha is therefore best approached as a productive meeting point between evidence types. It opens questions about travel, language and how distant societies named one another. Keeping those distinctions visible allows the connection with the Indus world to remain compelling without turning a strong historical argument into an unsupported claim of complete certainty.
